replace: As summarized by a 2004 narrative review of tablet analyses (Parrott, 2004), what is sold as ecstasy has mostly held MDMA but not always, and the amount in a tablet has varied widely.

What is sold as ecstasy has mostly held MDMA but not always, and the amount in a tablet has varied widely, both in tablet analyses up to about 2002, as summarized by a 2004 narrative review (Parrott, 2004), and in tablets sold as ecstasy that people chose to bring to drug-checking services in five European countries in 2008–2013 (Brunt et al., 2017).

The limits are that no study used random sampling, most samples were brought in by people who use drugs or came from amnesty bins, seizures of uniform batches may overstate purity, a US service that charged $100 a pill probably over-represented unusual pills, and the data end around 2002, so they do not describe tablets now.

In the drug-checking report, seven services in the Netherlands, Spain, Switzerland, Austria, Belgium and Portugal analysed 45,859 samples of all kinds in 2008–2013, 28,613 of them at the Dutch service; the tablet results come from five services. The share of tablets sold as ecstasy that held MDMA fell around 2009 and then rose again: read from the report's figure, it was about 19 in 100 in Austria, 30 in Spain, 47 in Switzerland and 64 in the Netherlands in 2009, and about 61 in Spain, 78 in Austria, 92 in the Netherlands, 95 in Switzerland and 100 in Belgium (a service with 244 samples of all kinds, reporting from 2011) in 2013. The average MDMA in a tablet, measured by four services, was about 61 to 74 mg in 2009 and about 103 to 114 mg in 2013 (read from the figure; Austria's lowest, about 43 mg, was in 2010): about 1.8 to 1.9 times as much in the Netherlands and about 1.4 to 1.6 times in Austria, Spain and Switzerland, so the report's statement that the amount approximately doubled, from 60–70 to 107–114 mg, fits the Netherlands only. These too are amounts measured in tablets, not amounts to take. The authors suggest, as speculation, that makers raised the amount after the 2009 shortage or to compete with new drugs, and say, with no data on harms in this report, that higher-dose tablets raise the risk of adverse effects and overdose, especially when people do not expect them. New psychoactive substances turned up in tablets sold as ecstasy or powders sold as MDMA, among them mCPP (listed for 2008 by all five services in the report's table), methylone, mephedrone and dextromethorphan, and, only in the Netherlands, 4-FA, PMMA and PMA; the range found grew over the years. Like the review, the report does not look at other reasons for feeling little or at what happens when people then take more. It gives no sample numbers by year or service and no intervals; the services used different laboratory methods; and the Dutch service identified a tablet from a batch already analysed at least three times by its logo, size, weight, colour and a quick colour test, and gave the batch's average content without a new analysis, without the report saying whether such tablets are counted in its figures. Neither source tests whether a logo tells what a tablet holds. The review's limits are that no study used random sampling, most samples were brought in by people who use drugs or came from amnesty bins, seizures of uniform batches may overstate purity, and a US service that charged $100 a pill probably over-represented unusual pills; the drug-checking samples, too, were brought in by people who chose to test, and the review's data end around 2002 and the drug-checking data in 2013, so neither describes tablets now.
Amounts are contents of tablets, not amounts to take.

Brunt et al. (2017), drug-checking services in six European countries (tablet results from five), 2008–2013 (45,859 samples of all kinds, 28,613 at the Dutch service; no numbers by year or service), read from the figures (approximate): share of tablets sold as ecstasy containing MDMA in 2009, Austria about 19, Spain 30, Switzerland 47, Netherlands 64 in 100; in 2013, Spain about 61, Austria 78, Netherlands 92, Switzerland 95, Belgium 100. Average MDMA per tablet (four services): 2009 about 61 (Netherlands) to 74 mg (Austria); 2013 about 103 (Spain) to 114 mg (Netherlands); Austria about 43 mg in 2010; from 2009 to 2013 about 1.8 to 1.9 times in the Netherlands and 1.4 to 1.6 times in Austria, Spain and Switzerland (editors' calculation from these readings); the text gives 60–70 mg (2009) and 107–114 mg (2013), described as approximately doubled. Amounts are contents of tablets, not amounts to take.

set.plain: Ecstasy is often MDMA, but not always, and one tablet can hold much more than another. A 2004 review of tablet tests put the share holding MDMA at about 90 to 98 in 100 from the 1980s to the early 1990s, about 50 to 80 in 100 in the mid-1990s, and nearly all by the early 2000s. The rest held related drugs such as MDA or MDEA, other substances such as ketamine, caffeine or paracetamol, or nothing active. Later, drug-checking services in five European countries tested tablets that people brought them. In 2009 only about 19 to 64 in 100 tablets sold as ecstasy held MDMA, depending on the country; by 2013 it was about 61 to 100 in 100. Newer drugs such as mCPP or PMMA turned up in some ecstasy. The MDMA measured in tablets ran from none to about 150 mg in the older tests; in the newer ones the average rose from about 61 to 74 mg in 2009 to about 103 to 114 mg in 2013, nearly double in the Netherlands and less elsewhere (measurements, not amounts to take). Some people feel a tablet did little. One possible reason, which these findings fit, is that it held less MDMA than the last one, or none. People in an Australian survey thought about 1 in 4 or 5 tablets was a dud. Neither source looks at other reasons, such as tolerance, or at what happens when people then take more. The samples were not random, the newest data end in 2013, the older figures reach us second-hand, and neither source tested whether a tablet's logo tells you what's inside.
set.population: Tablets and capsules sold or submitted as ecstasy (or MDMA) and analysed in laboratories or by testing services in the USA (to 1985), the Netherlands (1993 to 1999), north-east Italy (1995 to 2000), the UK, the Czech Republic and a US website (to 2002), with surveys of people who use ecstasy on how they judged tablet quality, all as summarized in a 2004 narrative review; and tablets sold as ecstasy that people brought to drug-checking services in the Netherlands, Spain, Switzerland, Austria and Belgium in 2008–2013 (shares containing MDMA from five services, amounts from four)
set.exposure: Being sold or submitted as ecstasy or MDMA; contents found by laboratory analysis (quick tests first in the Dutch series; in 2008–2013 gas or liquid chromatography or thin-layer chromatography by service, with Dutch tablets from batches already analysed identified by logo, physical features and a colour test)
set.comparator: Earlier and later periods and different countries, within the review and between the drug-checking services; no random sample and no reference standard
set.outcome: Share of tablets holding MDMA, related drugs (MDA, MDEA), amphetamines or other substances, including new psychoactive substances (2008–2013); milligrams of MDMA per tablet
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: No random sampling: samples were brought in by people, taken from amnesty bins or seized, and a paid test service over-represented odd tablets; the review itself calls its estimates very approximate. The 2008–2013 samples were also brought in by people who chose to test, at services of very different size, analysed by different laboratory methods, and the report does not say whether Dutch tablets identified by logo and a colour test, and given their batch's average, are counted in its figures (card sc_brunt_2017: JBI, high risk as a measure of national markets).
set.grade.domains.indirectness.note: The pre-2002 figures are second-hand (the primary analyses were not read); the 2008–2013 figures are primary but come from European services that people chose to use and end in 2013, so neither answers what tablets hold now, or elsewhere.
set.grade.domains.imprecision.note: Ranges without intervals; several older series are small and the review's own estimates overlap; the 2008–2013 yearly values are read from figures, with no sample numbers by year or service, some from small services (Belgium, 244 samples of all kinds over three years).
set.grade.reasoning: Descriptive findings from observational analyses start low (METHODS 6.3); risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision each take a level, and the result is very low. The qualitative finding (tablets sold as ecstasy are often but not always MDMA, and the amount varies) is better supported than any single percentage. Status replicated: independent series in the US, the Netherlands, Italy, the UK and the Czech Republic, as the review reports them, and drug-checking services in five European countries in 2008–2013 point the same way (METHODS 6.4); the Dutch monitoring system appears in both the review (1993 to 1999) and the 2008–2013 report, so for the Netherlands the two are one system's successive data, not independent replication. Round pdf-2026-11-14: the claim no longer rests only on a narrative review, since Brunt et al. (2017) adds primary drug-checking data; it stays at draft until the new anchors are checked by a second reader. The report's statement that MDMA per tablet approximately doubled holds only for the Netherlands by its own Figure 8, and the claim says so. Neither source tests whether a logo tells what a tablet holds. The claim is worded as a description of the years covered and gives no advice; the amounts are tablet contents, not doses.
set.verification.flag_note: The pre-2002 part rests on Parrott (2004) as summarized; none of the primary tablet analyses was read (Renfroe 1986; Spruit 2001; Schifano 2000; Cole et al. 2002; Palenicek et al. 2002; Ramsey et al. 2001), and none has a reference record here. SECTION: the brief put this claim in section 7, which only the senior author may write (the validator fails a section 7 claim whose drafter is not the senior author); it is staged in section 2, where METHODS 8 places drug-checking findings and adulterants. Move it if you prefer. VROLIJK 2022 (Vrolijk et al., Drugs, Habits and Social Policy, doi 10.1108/dhs-01-2022-0003) is still being obtained and was not used; it would add 2012 to 2021, a defined European sample (tablets sent to drug-checking services) and milligrams per tablet over time. RULE 0: the 'I barely felt it' paragraph is met for why it can happen (a weaker, empty or different tablet) but neither source has data on what happens when people take more; the editor may link the laboratory repeat-dose claim (cl_mdma_redose_cardiovascular) and the tolerance claim (cl_mdma_tolerance_chronic) from this one. Round pdf-2026-11-14 (AI reader 684): Brunt et al. (2017), read in full from the online-first PDF, adds 2008–2013 drug-checking results (five anchors, ai-located, awaiting a second reader). Whether a logo tells what a tablet holds is not tested by either source: it needs Vogels et al. (2009, Addiction 104, 2057) and Brunt and Niesink (2011, Drug Testing and Analysis 3, 621), which Brunt et al. cite for the reliability of recognising tablets by logo and which are not on file. The senior author's approval of 25 October 2026 was given on version 0.1.2.

evidence_add.locator: Materials and methods › Colourimetric drug tests, single paragraph (PDF p. 2); Discussion, 9th and 10th paragraphs (PDF p. 9)
evidence_add.extracted: For each tablet, logo, diameter, thickness, weight, colour and groove were recorded; a tablet from a batch already analysed by GC-MS at least three times was taken as identified by its colour-test result and these features, and the person who brought it was given the batch's average content and range. The authors state that this recognition has proven very reliable in the Netherlands, citing earlier work, with no data in this paper, and do not say whether such tablets are counted in the figures. Limits they state: people using the services do not necessarily represent all people who use drugs; the services differed greatly in scale; an unknown proportion of people are not interested in testing; the laboratories used different techniques and sensitivities and reported purity as salt or base, which may have led to underreporting of new substances and adulterants.
